Issued at 151 AM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

500mb ridge axis to fold overhead through Thursday as an initial 
northern stream wave cresting the ridge flattens and passes through 
northern Ontario. Surface high pressure over the mid Atlantic 
coupled with the surface low associated with the northern stream 
wave will continue to drum up breezy SW winds that will pump 
unseasonably mild air into the the region through the week's end 
owing to a pinched pressure gradient. The initial wave / surface low 
will crest the 500mb ridge axis Thursday, forcing a decaying, 
moisture-starved cold front through the region Thursday evening. In 
the wake of the front, the ridge rapidly recovers and peaks overhead 
again by Friday night - Saturday. Another northern stream wave, this 
one a bit more robust, passes through Saturday night, drumming up 
more breezy conditions Saturday before forcing a much stronger cold 
front through the region Sunday, bringing a return to seasonably 
cold air across the region for the start of Thanksgiving Week.

Details: 

Temps and Winds: Dry weather to prevail through much of Saturday as 
northern Michigan finds itself sandwiched between airmasses. Result 
will be unseasonable warmth through Saturday... with highs in the 
50s to near 60 (in downsloping locales like NE lower and the TVC 
area) today. Warmth spikes for Thursday as prefrontal warm advection 
and efficient mixing owing to a further pinching of the pressure 
gradient (SW winds expected to gust 25-35mph) sends highs soaring 
into the 60s for most of northern lower and mid-upper 50s for our 
friends in the eastern Yoop. Aforementioned dry frontal passage will 
"stunt" the warmth into Friday as winds turn more calm in the wake 
of the system, topping out anywhere from the low-to-mid 50s in 
eastern upper, and upper 50s to lower 60s in northern lower. Warmth 
peaks Saturday as the next system approaches, once again pinching 
the pressure gradient (SW gusts again 25-35mph) and sending 
prefrontal warm advection into overdrive. Highs in eastern upper top 
out in the upper 50s to near 60, with most of northern lower topping 
out in the low-to-mid 60s, perhaps pushing upper 60s in downsloping 
locales. 

Cold frontal passage Saturday night into Sunday will lead to falling 
temperatures through the day, and by Sunday evening, the return of 
much more seasonable November weather is restored as a biting NW 
wind (gusts 25-30mph) pumps in colder Canadian air. Temps start in 
the 40s and 50s Sunday, and probably drop into the 30s by sunset for 
most. For the rest of the week, highs in the 30s and lows in the 20s 
are set to prevail, though some uncertainty remains on the longevity
of the colder weather closer to the Thanksgiving holiday itself.
Owing to regency biases, this is certainly going to generate a shock,
and probably an unhealthy amount of griping from warm weather lovers,
but the reality is, our average highs by next Monday span from 37
to 42... so this upcoming airmass for next week is statistically
far more normal than the warmth we are about to experience through
Saturday. 

Rain / Precip Chances: What was once looking like a shot at rain 
chances Thursday just a few days ago now appears to be quite the 
pipe dream. The Thursday system looks to pass well to our north, 
failing to ingest available moisture to our south, which will be 
gobbled up by a pesky tropical origin system lazily spinning over 
the southeastern CONUS. Meanwhile, the next ensuing system will be 
occluding considerably as it moves into Minnesota, which will likely 
result in us seeing a period of high based, elevated convection 
Saturday night into Sunday as the front finally passes through. 
Thunder potential looks muted at this point, but in the event we can 
actually manifest some elevated instability, could see that nosing 
into the picture in the coming days. For now, longer range guidance 
is pessimistic toward the idea. As such, amplification biases in 
longer term guidance leads to struggles with these systems that 
occlude into oblivion to our west and slowly meander through the 
Great Lakes. That being said, longer term guidance's idea of a lack 
of overlap with low level synoptic moisture and the coldest air from 
this system leading to a failure of lake induced instability 
generation seems like a fair bet to mute any sort of backside lake 
effect snows with this system Sunday night into Monday... likely 
being unimpactful if any. The dry nature of the airmass will also 
lead to a lack of organized precipitation chances into next week.
